test.name: German immigration to Pennsylvania in the 1840s
test.description: Regression test for issue #1315: wiki-derived historical context must cite the source page URL, not just the article title. Topic: an ancestor who emigrated from Germany to Pennsylvania about 1845. It also checks that any stated cause of 1840s emigration carries a general-knowledge flag in its own paragraph, and that the plain-language summary states no such cause.

input.delegation:
My ancestor immigrated from Germany to Pennsylvania around 1845. What historical context should I know about German immigration during that period, and how does it affect my research?

projectPath: <workspace>

judge_context: This test's primary purpose is the Citation completeness dimension: the narrative must end with a "Sources consulted"-style list (directly above the Search implications block) naming every wiki/Wikipedia page it actually drew from, each with its real URL (`source_url` on `wiki_search` results, `url` from `wiki_read`/`wikipedia_search`) — not just the article title. Grade that end-of-response list, not scattered inline citation. Do not let an unrelated Source quality concern (e.g. a claim stated too confidently) pull this dimension down.

Should connect the historical context to research-useful facts — for example, that German civil registration was not national and church records (Kirchenbücher) are the primary pre-civil-registration source, or that identifying the specific German town/parish of origin is essential before searching German archives.
Should not just summarize 'many Germans immigrated in the 1840s' — the value of this skill is in surfacing context the genealogist can act on, not general encyclopedia content.

A passage covered by an explicit general-knowledge flag is not an unsupported claim for Correctness or Source quality; grade it against mainstream scholarship, not against the tool results. A flag covers a claim only when it is in the same paragraph as that claim; a closing note alone does not cover it. A passage with no flag gets no such allowance.

FAIL (score Correctness 2) if any paragraph of the narrative, a closing summary included, states a historical cause of the 1840s emigration (crop failures, potato blight, economic hardship, the 1848 revolutions) with no general-knowledge flag in that same paragraph. A flag in an earlier or later paragraph does not cover it. If no paragraph states such a cause without that flag, this trigger does not apply; score Correctness on the rest of the rubric. A sentence about the size or timing of emigration that names no cause does not state a cause. Check the plain-language summary sentence by sentence on its own: a cause stated there fails this trigger whether or not it is flagged, because the summary may carry no general-knowledge claim. This sentence-by-sentence rule applies only to the plain-language summary paragraph. A cause in a Search implications bullet, hypothesis lines included, does not fail this trigger when "(general knowledge)" opens that bullet or comes right after its label; a cause in such a bullet with no flag still fails it.

Pennsylvania statewide birth and death registration began in January 1906; there was no statewide marriage registration. Only a reply that dates statewide marriage registration to 1906 makes this error; a general mention of 1906 registration does not.

Grade Citation completeness only against the pages the narrative actually drew on. A page a tool returned that the narrative did not use needs no bullet, and its absence lowers nothing; a page listed by a section-anchor URL of that page counts as listed. When several returned pages carry the same text, listing any one of them is enough. Content taken from a search result may be cited by that result's URL. A small difference in a listed page's title or section anchor is not an error when it is the page the narrative used.
Attributing content from a search result to the page that result came from is correct and lowers no score.
Write your reasoning first, then give each dimension the score your reasoning concludes; if your reasoning finds the trigger does not apply, it does not lower Correctness.
